segments.text: - So at the end of the day, you know,

when people see this, they
gotta get interested in it,
and so I'm wondering,

what has been the response from
other folks in the industry?
- Yeah, it's been...

Overall, I think the
reaction's been one of,
you know, a mix of surprise
in that we can actually do this,
but also excitement in the technology.

I've had people literally
ask me for samples

because they didn't believe
me that we were kind of doing
what I was saying we were doing, right?

So it's always fun to
send something to somebody
and be like, "I told you!" But...
(gentle electronic music)
- Hello, everyone,

and welcome to the
Altium "OnTrack" podcast,
I'm your host, Zach Peterson,

today, we're talking with Tyler
Richards, founder of uFab.
Tyler founded uFab, and his systems
take desktop printing to the next level,

and I wouldn't even really
call it desktop printing
because these machines are really
a whole different beast altogether,

so I'm very happy to be
talking with Tyler today.
- Yeah, thanks for having me.

- Yeah, I'm glad that
somebody introduced you to me
because I have considered many times
to get a desktop etching or laser...

You know, laser etching
system or whatever it is,
and I haven't really viewed them
as kind of, like, a production thing,

and when I saw your
system, I said to myself,

"Okay, this feels,
like, production grade."

- Yeah, and that's kind of
what we want to go for, right?
Is, like, fab quality

without necessarily
needing a fab to do it.

- And the other I noticed
is, looking at your system,
it didn't look like you...
It...
I mean, you need some kind of facility,
but not like the, you know,
50,000 square foot kind of facility

that you typically
associate with a PCB fab.
- Yeah, yeah, it's really interesting,

so we operate out of a
1,300 square foot facility,

and one of our customers,
who's also using our machine,
it's essentially a cabinet inside of a...
About a 500 square foot lab...

Development lab, so, I mean,
maybe not desktop printing,
but more like cabinet printing. (laughs)
- Sure, sure.
Well, before we get into the uFab system,

if you could, just tell us
a little bit about yourself
and how you got started in electronics.
- Yeah, I...

So I've been kind of
obsessed with electronics
from a very early age,
like, you know, back in...

I was, like, 10 years
old, and Radio Shack...

The local Radio Shack had just
started stalking Arduinos,
and so I got pretty obsessed with that,
I was kind of into the maker movement
and everything like that,
I subscribed to Make Magazine,
and so, you know, that kind of flourished,
and then, in high school, in about 2015,

I actually started doing
freelance design work,
so there was a platform called Upwork,

and they were relatively
new at the time, I believe,
and I found freelance design gigs
and was getting paid to do that
instead of getting a real job,

and did that pretty much up
through college actually,

and so I've just been doing
electronics my whole life.

- You know, I gotta be
honest, Upwork is how I found
some of my first consulting gigs

when I was getting out of
academia and going into industry,

although I was not a high
school student at the time,

so that's very cool that
you were doing that.

- Well, I don't think
most of my customers knew
that I was a high school student,
so it came as a shock to them sometimes

when we called and then
they got, you know,

this little kid basically
doing their board design,

but yeah, Upwork's an
interesting platform for sure,

I think there's a lot of
freelance platforms out there now,
so it's a interesting world.
- So you've gone from, you know,

freelance board designing
when you're younger,

all the way up now to where
you have your own company,
you have this impressive system,

if you could tell us about
uFab and your product.
- Yeah, yeah, so I typically start

by talking about why I started
uFab in the first place,

and, you know, I want
you to kind of step back

to, like, 2020 when the
COVID lockdown started,

and, you know, every single
PCB fab shut down, right?

And you couldn't get
stuff into the country
and it was just terrible, right?

And as a freelancer, it
was actually my fault,
according to my customers,

that we couldn't get boards
into the country, right?

Because they had no idea
about supply chains,

and so that's when I started
really thinking about, like,

in-house circuit board
production and rapid fab,
and so towards the end of university,

I essentially pitched
this idea of rapid fab

and was able to kind of
get an angel investor
and get some fundraising done
to build out this prototype machine,
and the real focus was commercial...
You know, commercial-grade fabrication

as fast as possible
without using, you know,
traditional chemical etching,
like ferric chloride or cupric chloride,

and so what ended up
happening was I essentially...
The first product that we built
was a laser manufacturing machine,

we call it the PCBee, spelled
P-C-B-E-E, and it'll...
It is a ultra-rapid circuit board printer,
so we can print multi-layer boards
in about four hours or less
without using chemical etchants
or really any of the kind of nasty stuff
associated with traditional fab.

- So without revealing any
of the proprietary stuff,

if you could tell us
what makes the PCB system

different from some of the
existing desktop systems,

'cause, you know, you have
stuff out there that's like,

right, you can do, like,
laser etching, right?

So there are some of those
machines that's basically,
you know, numerically controlled laser,

and then, you also have 3D
printing systems out there,
but, I mean, those systems are, like,
prohibitively expensive,

you know, they put 'em
in a basement somewhere

and work on, you know,
parts for satellites
with those systems,
so what makes your system different,
whether it's the technology
or the user interface or whatever?
- Yeah, I mean, it's a lot actually,

you know, technology,
user interface, et cetera,

I think the biggest
thing is that, you know,

we aim to support as broad of
a design space as possible,
so we're really focused on, you know,

if you utilize our machine,
you can take the boards

that you've, you know, designed,
iterated on our machine

and take that design
without any kind of changes
and put it into mass manufacturing,

so that really starts with
utilizing the same materials
that traditional fabs use,
so, like, we're using FR-4,

we buy our flex materials
from DuPont and Panasonic,
you know, we're buying Rogers materials
for, like, ceramic boards,
and, you know, so these are, like,
full copper circuit boards
as opposed to, like, centered metals

or conductive pastes or
something like that where,

you know, you can kind of run
into impedance design issues

where, like, a conductive
paste obviously doesn't have

the same impedance
characteristics as, say,
a copper trace, right?
And then, going beyond that, you know,
we really try to focus on making boards
that are identical in function and spec
as a traditional fab,
and so, you know, that's one aspect of it,

there's also the integration
of the ecosystem,

so one of the big complaints
that I heard was, like,
"The software is impossible to use,"
or, "You need, like, hours of training
to understand how to use it,"

so we built out our software
to essentially step you

through every single
production step with videos,

text explanations, you know,
infographics, et cetera,
to make sure that you're not lost

or, you know, you don't
need to spend hours
training somebody on using the system,

and then, you know,
there's some other things
that we do small scale, we don't try to...
We don't try and sell a gigantic machine,
you know, things like that,

we have miniature presses,
like, desktop presses
for PCB lamination, which is fun,

and yeah, no tooling, no
masking, no chemical etching,

I mean, we really try to
make it as easy as possible.
- Yeah, it sounds like it,
especially eliminating the etchants,
I think that's really the big one
that the desktop systems,

or as you called it, the
cabinet level systems
or the 3D printing systems, you know,
they always talk about that

and making it more
environmentally friendly

and sustainable and all
of that kind of stuff,
and yeah, the etchants are a challenge,

if you look what some of the
makers do at home, you know,
there really isn't a lot of...

I don't think there's a
lot of concern for safety,
they're still using etchants at home.

- (laughs) Yeah, it's a
little concerning when I see,

you know, posts on forums and
stuff, people talking about

just pouring ferric
chloride down the drain,
I'm like, "Oh, gosh, your pipes
are probably not there anymore." (laughs)
- Yeah, that's true, that's true.
So you've mentioned a...
I think a couple types of designs
that the system can support, right?
You brought up flex materials,

and then, you'd even mentioned
Rogers, so PTFE materials,
and then, can you do things like ceramic?

Can you do metal core,
those types of designs?
- Yeah, so we...
I've been hard pressed to find a material

that we haven't been able
to print onto, honestly,
I've printed on...
So I've got some samples here
if you'd like me to show, but...
- [Zach] Oh, yeah, absolutely.

- Yeah. So this is a 3D
printer stepper driver,
let's see if that comes across there,

but this is just a traditional
FR-4 board, you know,
so this was done entirely on our machine,
the drilling through holes,
silkscreen, solder mask, et cetera.
- That's the next thing I was gonna ask,
was the silkscreen and the solder mask,

you're actually doing
it inside the machine?
- Yes, yes, which...
And no masking, which is really cool,
and we can talk about that in just a bit,

but, you know, we're also
doing things like flex and...

Let's see here, I don't think
I have a Rogers sample here,

but we've printed on,
like, Rogers 4000, TMM6,
you know, I...
Again, like, I've...
It's been really tough to find a material

we haven't printed on,
and what's cool is that,

you know, again, going back to
that manufacturability idea,

we get down to about 50 micron,
or two mil feature sizes,
so, you know, BGA parts,
high density designs, all that fun stuff.
- This...
That makes it pretty competitive
with some of the more advanced processing

that's available from
traditional manufacturers,
'cause I, I mean, I've had designs
that are pushing towards two mil
and they've got no bid at one place

and, you know, you have
to take 'em somewhere else

and they have a process
that'll do two mils

or I've had to, you know, put
it with someone in Taiwan,

but you're like, "Yeah, two
mils, go for it." (laughs)

- Well, you know, it's
actually kind of funny,
so our laser can actually...
The spot size itself is about 20 microns,

so theoretically, we could
get smaller than two mil,
but that... (laughs)

If people start asking for
bids on those projects,
I get a little scared,

'cause it's probably some
sort of very specific design.

- No, that's understandable,
I mean, what...?
So, you know, that's the density, right?
Is two mil in terms of feature size,
and then, two mil spacing, correct?
- Yeah, yeah.

- Okay. And then, what
about, like, via sizes?
What about layer counts?

- Yeah, so we use the same
laser system for drilling,

so we can actually get
down to about seven mil,
eight mil minimum drill size,
these drills...
These vias are plated,
we have a proprietary plating system,

which I can talk about
for a really long time,

but yeah, so we have
a rapid plating system
that allows us to do, you know,
seven, eight mil vias, and...

I'm sorry, I'm blanking,
your other question...
Oh, layer counts.
- [Zach] Yeah, yeah.

- Yeah, so we've confirmed
up to four layers,
we're qualifying six-plus right now,
I mean, there isn't really any reason
why we can't do higher layer counts,
I can show you right here,

so our carrier boards that
get fed into the machine,
they actually have fiducials
and kind of locking pins built into them,

so it's very simple to,
you know, take your board

and take your next panel
and stick them together
and laminate them together
to build your stack up,
and so, you know, really, the thing
that's been holding me back thus far

has just been time and
qualification steps,
you know, we're a startup,
so we have to move pretty quickly.

We're also qualifying
rigid-flex right now, actually,
which has been exciting,
I mean, if we can do the rigid boards

and we can do the flexible
boards, why not put 'em together?
- Yeah, you preempted my question there,
was if you can do rigid-flex.
So the overall process here

is basically somebody
takes your feeder boards,
they're doing it layer by layer,
at the end of it, they're gonna do the...
They're gonna press everything together,

then they're gonna put
it back in the machine,
go through your plating process
to plate all their through-holes,
and then, that's it, they're done.
- Yeah, and beyond the, you know,

the solder masking and
silkscreening steps,

or with flex, that's
typically a coverlay process,
and we're just using, like,
a DuPont Pyralux coverlay there,
so, you know, very traditional materials,
and then, yeah,

you have your functional
board really quickly.
- So then I assume that means

you also have support
for blinded-buried vias.
- So I actually...

Again, that's another thing
that we're qualifying,

there isn't any reason
why we shouldn't be able
to do those things, but again, it's...
You know, we have to kind of

structure our product
development, and that's, you know,

a little bit farther down the
line on our qualifications,

but yeah, I mean, there shouldn't
be a reason why we can't.

- Now, I have a question for
you here also about the vias,

so, you know, what you're doing
with your through-holes is,

you know, you're drilling
through layer by layer,
and then, laminating,

and then, you're plating through
on those hole walls, right?
It's...
But it's not like a, how do I put this?

It's not like stacking vias
to form a through-hole, right?

Because you're actually
plating the entire wall
all in one run.

- Yeah, so we can do
the drilling beforehand,
we can do the drilling afterwards,
you can do intermediate drilling steps

because, yeah, when you're
building that stack up,
you're obviously gonna have your laminate
in between your vias, right?
So you need to punch out that laminate.
Typically, especially right now,
since we're not doing blinded-buried,
we do the drilling stuff last

so that we can laminate
everything together,

and then, do a single drill
operation to then plate,

but yeah, you can do it
a lot of different ways.
- And then, is there any layer thickness

or board thickness
restriction with your system?

Because normally with,
like, laser drilling,
there's, you know, aspect ratio limits

depending on, you know,
the diameter of the hole
you're trying to place, right?
And then, if...

Obviously, if you go
to, like, really small,
you know, laser-drilled microvias,
you've got some serious depth limitations,
but you're all the way up

at, you know, eight-mil,
seven-mil diameter,
so I would imagine you could probably get

pretty far above one on
your drilling aspect ratio?
- Yeah, I...
So this is, like, a...

This is a 1.6-millimeter,
you know, board here,
and, I mean, we etch through...
We drill through these no problem, we...
The optical system that we've built
has allowed us to be able

to drill through these
materials relatively easily
with pretty high aspect ratios.
- And then, what's the maximum size
of a PCB you can print, or how...?

I guess you're feeding in
these feeder panels, right?

So that's kind of where
you're starting from,
so how big are those panels?

- Yeah, so right now, we
have two configurations

that we sell, we have a
five-by-five-inch printer
and a six-by-six-inch printer,
but what's really interesting...
Thing...
What we've really seen a lot of demand for
is a full-panel printer, actually,
so there isn't really any technical reason

why we can't print across
an entire print panel
beyond just the build of the machine,
the mechanics of the machine,

because the actual operation
scales quite nicely,
so what we're doing right now
is we're actually building a...
Essentially, a fab in a box

where you can print a
circuit board on a full panel

and do the etching, the
drilling, the lamination, the...

You know, the silkscreen
solder mask, et cetera,

but right now, it is
five-inch-by-five-inch
or six-inch-by-six-inch.
- So yeah, so you could basically do

a small panel of, you know,
smaller boards, right?
If you had little,

you know, let's say
half-inch-by-one-inch boards,

you can make your own
panel and put it in there.
- Yeah, and the goal is in the near-term,

we don't have that size
restriction anymore
and we can just, you know, take a panel
from a manufacturer and process it fully.
- Okay, okay, so if somebody did that,
they had, you know, these small boards
on your, you know, six-by-six-inch feeders
and they put them through your system,

what de-panelization
features can you support?
Will they have to, like, plan

to, like, mill out a route
path on a separate machine,

and then, maybe have mouse
bytes to do de-panelization?
- So yeah, we actually...
Again, because the laser can do drilling,
we do the de-panelization in the machine,
so, you know, traditionally,

if you think of, like, a
V-score or something like that
where you're kinda limited
by, like, the linearity of the boards
or, you know, with milling, right?
You have to worry about your bit breaking
or something like that,

we can just drill
straight out of the panels
so you can get really, really close...

You know, you can keep everything
relatively close together,
so, like, I've got a panel...
This is a flex panel that I processed

and I've kind of done some
other stuff to it as well,
but, you know, these are all flex PCBs

that we kept about a
millimeter from each other,

and we just drilled
them out with the laser
and, you know, called it a day. (laughs)

- Nice, nice. No, that's
really cool, right?
'Cause you can do...
Just do it all in one system again,

and I know that, you know,
some of those other methods

with, like, you know,
milling out a route path

or, you know, god forbid
you have to do V-scoring
can get pretty inaccurate,

especially when you, you
know, take this thing to scale

and, you know, they're just
kind of slicing through
real quick with that pizza cutter.
(Tyler laughing)
- Yeah, yeah, and I've seen a lot of cases
where people put their traces,

you know, right up on
the edge of the board,

and then, the traces get
destroyed by a V-score machine,

or, you know, a router,
or something like that,

so this is really nice
for designs that have,

you know, pretty tight
tolerances around the edges.

- So I'm interested to know,
what is the cost comparison
to working with your machine

versus going through
a traditional process?
Because, you know, the...
Your type of machine is the kind of thing

that I think proponents
of U.S. PCB manufacturing,

myself being one of those,
would look at and say, you know,
"Hey, maybe this is..."

You know, "Maybe we
need to totally rethink

the whole fab process and
focus on something different,"
and, you know, you're offering

what looks like a pretty
viable alternative,
you know, you talk about scaling it out
to larger panel sizes,

which I think, you know,
makes perfect sense,
but at the end of the day, you know,

if a company was gonna,
you know, build a facility
with 100 of these printers,

they've gotta see how it
pencils out financially,
so how does all that cost compare?

- Yeah, so it's actually
really interesting because...

Right, so take, for instance,
the chemical waste, right?
Associated with traditional PCB fab.
In our case, right, on a panelized...

On a panel printer, you're not
paying for that chemical...

Those chemicals themselves,
but you're also not paying

for the waste disposal
fees associated with that,

you're not paying for the
licensure to utilize those fees,

you're not, you know, paying
the insurance associated

with having those chemicals
in your facility, right?
So, you know, there's an economic argument
associated with that,

but there's also, like, an
environmental one as well,

you know, a lot of these
chemicals are hard to get rid of,

dissolved coppers or,
you know, copper ions
are super, super toxic to aquatic life,
but, you know, what I find really fun
is, you know, our proto printer

runs on a 120-volt,
15-amp wall outlet, right?
So the actual electrical consumption

associated with etching
these boards is quite small,
I think our current proto printer

only draws about 800
watts peak from the wall,

and so, you can imagine
scaling that to a panel,

the electrical cost is
actually not that bad
compared to, you know, what it costs
to run an etchant bath,
and a large mill, and all that stuff,
so it's really interesting,

and, you know, I think
another consideration

is, like, the CO2 associated
with shipping boards
across the Pacific Ocean, right?
So if you're buying boards from overseas
and shipping them to the States,
there's a cost to that as well,

so it's a really interesting
thing, not to mention the CapEx

associated with creating
a facility, right?

Which, again, I could talk
about that all day. (laughs)
- (laughs) Yeah, yeah,
well, there's a couple of points
I think that you highlighted
that are really interesting here too,

which is, you know, you mentioned
the environmental factor,
I would imagine that that expands
the number of places you could produce,

and because you've eliminated
all those etchants,
you've probably eliminated
a lot of environmental regulations
that you would have to follow
in certain parts of the country,
so it expands the number of locations

where you could produce, you
don't just have to produce

in places that are much
friendlier to manufacturing
and maybe don't have the same level
of environmental restrictions
that you do in other parts of the country,

and then, the other thing
that I think is interesting
is it might allow you to, you know,
produce closer to your customers,

so you brought up the
shipping and logistics aspect

and, you know, if you can
produce closer to the customer,
of course, you've eliminated all of that.
- Yeah, I mean, that's a great point,
especially, you know, the location thing,

I'm based in St. Louis,
Missouri right now,
and, you know, it didn't even...
I guess because I didn't have to go
seek out those permits and everything
'cause we're not using chemicals,

it didn't even occur to me that
it's kind of a special thing
that there's a PCB manufacturer
nestled in the center of St. Louis,
so yeah, I think that's a great point.
- Okay, so yeah, this is the kind of thing

where, you know, I think
it makes a lot of sense
to set up a lot of smaller facilities
closer to your customers
rather than set up one big facility,
try to navigate the permitting process,

and then, ship boards
all over the country.
- Yeah, I...

One of the examples
I've had mentioned to me

is, like, the airline industry
and the hub-and-spoke model
versus the point-to-point model,
you know, the efficiency
in kind of making manufacturing smaller...
In, you know, smaller batches, but closer
is a very compelling argument.
- So at the end of the day,
you know, when people see this,
they gotta get interested in it,

and so, I'm wondering
what has been the response
from other folks in the industry?
- Yeah, it's been...

Overall, I think the
reaction's been one of,
you know, a mix of surprise
in that we can actually do this,
but also excitement in the technology.

I've had people literally
ask me for samples

because they didn't believe
me that we were kind of doing
what I was saying we were doing, right?

So it's always fun to
send something to somebody
and be like, "I told you!" But...
(people laughing)
But, you know, it's been cool to see
the excitement generated around this,
you know, we have a couple of,
you know, really interesting projects

that I can't talk about
right now, unfortunately,
but hopefully, you know,
on our LinkedIn or our website, we'll...
You'll see something soon,

but, you know, one of the
really interesting areas
has been the education space,

one of the things that I've
been told by professors
is that, you know, the current lead times
associated with production is...
Kind of makes circuit...

Teaching circuit board
design kind of difficult

in a 14-week, you know,
class period, right?
So bringing that production close to home

and getting rid of those
lead times would be huge

for educating the next
generation of engineers.
- If I could jump in on that...
Or on that lead time point, right?
The other factor of that is cost,
because there are quick-turn shops
that will do it in 48 hours, let's say,

but, like, you gotta really
throw some gobs of money at 'em

to get 'em to do it, and
that's also not really feasible

for, you know, printed
circuit board class.
- Yeah, yeah, I agree,

I mean, when you go to some
of these manufacturers,

they'll quote you 500 dollars
a board for rapid turn,
and, you know, one of the things

that we've been doing
recently, we have a...
Some production capability in our facility
for doing board runs,

so we actually offer a
24-hour quick-turn service,

so customers can actually
go to our website

and order boards, and get
them in 24 hours or less,
and we do the same thing with, like...
You know, we print stencils as well,
so it's very interesting and exciting,

and opens up a lot of new
avenues for doing business.
- Now, you know, there are some industries
that are pretty conservative, right?
There's, you know, of course,
military, aerospace, automotive,
I think those are the big three

where you could really
get a lot of growth,

but of course, there's
a lot of qualification

that goes into it, of
course, you know, human...

People's lives, you know,
depend on these electronics,
so, you know, you have to be able
to prove that it's reliable,
how far down that rabbit hole
of proving reliability have you gone?
- Yeah, I mean, I think...

We have talked to some
people in the defense space,
in the automotive space, and again, it...

You know, reliability is
the biggest thing there,

I think, you know, beyond
just the qualification

that we've done of, you
know, showing, you know,
cross-sections of boards and printed...
You know, printed boards, et cetera,

you know, I think just
printing more boards
and showing that it works is one of,
I feel like, the easiest ways

of showing that the
technology actually works,
but we're also...
You know, we're looking for partners
in those industries, honestly, right now,
people who are willing to say, you know,
"Hey, this is interesting.
Hey, this could totally change
how we do manufacturing.
Let's work on this together."

- Well, and one thing I
guess I'm getting into
in terms of reliability is a lot of times,

specs will quote, like, certain
